title: Indian IT Stocks Just Had Their Worst Month in Years — and the Threat Isn't Just Cyclical, It's Existential
excerpt: The Nifty IT index fell 9.6% in June as Accenture's guidance cut, AI cannibalization fears, and Middle East demand shocks converged into a perfect storm for the $315 billion sector that employs millions of NRIs.
body:
The Nifty IT index closed June down 9.6 percent — its worst monthly performance in years — as three forces converged to punish India's most globally visible sector. For the millions of NRIs who work in Indian IT, hold IT stocks, or whose H-1B careers were built on the industry's rise, the decline isn't just a portfolio problem. It's a signal that the industry's business model is being questioned at a fundamental level.

## The Accenture Shock

The immediate trigger was Accenture, the world's largest IT services company and a bellwether for Indian outsourcers. The company slashed its fiscal year 2026 revenue growth guidance to 3-4 percent, down from the previous 4-5 percent range, citing a $90 million revenue shortfall and $100 million in lost business from Middle East disruptions.

CEO Julie Sweet's acknowledgment that U.S. federal contracts had slowed significantly under the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative — with Accenture's Federal Services unit representing roughly 8 percent of global revenue — sent shockwaves through the sector. Indian IT firms, which derive more than half their revenue from the United States, saw the writing on the wall.

TCS fell over 5 percent. Infosys dropped more than 7 percent. The Nifty IT Index plunged more than 5 percent on the day of Accenture's results alone. By month's end, the sector had shed approximately $26 billion in market value.

## The AI Existential Question

But the cyclical demand weakness is only part of the story. The more corrosive force is the market's growing conviction that agentic AI could automate a significant portion of what IT services companies do.

Accenture's stock has plunged 50 percent from its January highs — from roughly $259 to around $125 per share — partly because investors are pricing in the possibility that its 700,000-person workforce could be partially displaced by AI tools. When Anthropic released new enterprise AI tools in February, IT services stocks fell across the board without any company-specific news.

JP Morgan's analysis is sobering. The investment bank says AI adoption in IT services will progress through three phases — deflation, digestion, and reflation — with GenAI-led productivity gains actively shrinking revenue before AI services become large enough to offset the drag. The critical detail: the "digestion phase" could extend beyond FY2029, meaning the structural headwind may persist for years.

An MOFSL report was blunter: "OpenAI's DeployCo and Anthropic's services company represent the first credible blueprint of the next-gen system integrator. This will not be a winner-takes-all market, but it will be a painful transition period for the existing book of business."

## The Broader Market Context

Indian markets as a whole fared much better. The Nifty 50 gained 1.4 percent in June and the Sensex rose 2.3 percent, powered by banking stocks that surged over 6 percent after the RBI extended subsidised forex swap facilities and eased rules on lending to non-residents. Pharma gained 4 percent. Brent crude's collapse — from $126 at its April peak to around $73 a barrel — eased inflation fears and stabilised the rupee, which posted its first quarterly gain in five quarters.

But IT was the outlier. While ten of 16 major sectors advanced in June, IT was the worst performer by a wide margin, with metals (down 6.9 percent) the only other significant decliner. The rupee's recovery, which typically boosts IT earnings on translation, couldn't offset the structural fears.

## What NRIs Need to Know

For Indian-Americans working in the IT services sector, this is not a distant stock market story. It touches three pressure points simultaneously.

**Employment risk.** Nomura's report emphasised that the West Asia conflict and AI disruption are combining to delay deal signings and ramp-ups, directly affecting headcount planning. TCS posted its first annual revenue decline in more than two decades. Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro all trimmed their FY27 revenue growth forecasts. Slower growth means slower hiring — and potentially the first meaningful layoff cycles in Indian IT since the 2008 financial crisis.

**Investment exposure.** IT stocks have traditionally been a core holding for NRI investors seeking exposure to India's global competitiveness. The Nifty IT index is near its 52-week low, and Citi has flagged that it still trades at a premium relative to Accenture's valuation — suggesting more downside is possible if earnings cuts materialise after Q1 results.

**H-1B and immigration.** The IT services model is inextricable from the H-1B visa system. If Indian IT companies face a structural — not cyclical — slowdown in U.S. revenue, the lobbying power and visa volume that has sustained the pipeline of Indian professionals into American tech companies could weaken in ways that reshape the diaspora's professional trajectory.

## A Painful Transition, Not a Death Sentence

The bull case still exists. Accenture itself posted record new bookings of $22.1 billion in Q2, including 41 clients with quarterly bookings above $100 million. It has partnered with OpenAI and Anthropic to position itself as an enterprise AI deployment layer — an acknowledgment that the transition is happening and must be led, not resisted.

Indian IT companies are not standing still either. But the sector that once seemed like an unstoppable engine of diaspora wealth creation is now navigating what JP Morgan calls "the most painful transition since the shift to cloud." Whether the industry emerges leaner and stronger — or permanently diminished — remains the defining question for NRI portfolios and careers alike.

*Sources: Reuters, Motley Fool, ainvest.com, The Hindu Business Line, Nomura, JP Morgan, MOFSL, Citi*
